before:
Recall that a linear transformation $T$ maps ${R}^{2}$ onto  ${R}^{2}$ if and only if 

$$
\text{rank}(T)=\text{rank}(T)=2
$$

and, according to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T)=\text{nullity}(T) & =2-\text{rank}(T) \\  & =2-2 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. The condition $\text{rank}(T)=2$ in ${R}^{2}$ is equivalent to

$$
\text{Im}(T)={R}^{2}.
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the condition $\text{nullity}(T)=0$ in ${R}^{2}$ is equivalent to 

$$
\text{Ker}(T)={0}.
$$

- Statement III is false. We have that 

$$
\text{nullity}(T)=0.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

before:
Recall that the standard Hermitian inner product over $C$ satisfies the following properties:

- It is linear in the first argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a+b,c⟩=⟨a,c⟩+⟨b,c⟩\,$ and $\,⟨\alpha a,b⟩=\alpha ⟨a,b⟩.$

- It is antilinear in the second argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,b+c⟩=⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c⟩\,$ and $\,⟨a,\alpha b⟩=\overset{―}{\alpha }⟨a,b⟩.$

- It has conjugate symmetry. For any $a,b\in {C}^{n},$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,b⟩=\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}.$

- It is positive-definite. For any $a\in {C}^{n},$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,a⟩$ is a non-negative real number, and $⟨a,a⟩=0$ if and only if $a=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. Notice that if $a=0$ then $⟨a,a⟩=0.$

- Statement II is false. The inner product over $C$ is a complex number in general.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, the inner product in ${C}^{n}$ is linear in the first argument. So, a constant multiple from the first argument can be factored out.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

before:
A square matrix $A$ is symmetric if it is equal to its transpose:

$$
A={A}^{T}
$$

Equivalently, ${a}_{ij}={a}_{ji}$ for all $i,j.$ In other words, $A$ is symmetric across its main diagonal.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. As a counterexample, consider the matrix 

$\,$ $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$

However, ${A}^{3}$ is not symmetric:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{3} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, for any two symmetric matrices $A$ and $B,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}(A+B)^{T} & ={A}^{T}+{B}^{T} \\  & =A+B.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, for any two symmetric matrices $A$ and $B,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-B)^{T} & ={A}^{T}-{B}^{T} \\  & =A-B.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

$$

$$

$$
